coherence.reasons: Both documents have a clean hierarchy. Y is tighter: its governing thought carries the payback condition (ACoS below 28.6%) and four section claims are each backed by two or three slide titles. Its one logical gap is that it says the ambition 'needs retail on top, later' and keeps a retail gate at 20% awareness and $10M Amazon sales, while its own slide 22 shows national retail in 2029 breaks payback and the margin floor; it only says the step 'needs its own case'. X organises everything around an explicit seven-condition test of the CEO's hypothesis, and its retail trigger closes that gap by requiring a plan that fits the guardrails. X has small inconsistencies of its own: peak-cash ranges quoted differently across slides (−$1.9M to −$3.9M, −$1.9M to −$3.2M, 'worst tested' $6.4M, a $4M envelope), and a slide title saying $40M needs 'only about 1%' of the market alongside the conclusion that no route reaches $40M by 2030. These roughly offset.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation: Amazon-led entry in 2027 with gates, retail-led rejected on the board's own constraints, and the $40M ambition acknowledged as out of reach. X weighs the trade-offs more fully. It puts the ambition-versus-guardrails choice to the board explicitly (re-phase to about 2032, or relax the guardrails and accept at least $21M peak cash and Mooncrest-type risk). It quantifies a stalled launch (−$6.3M by 2030, capped near $3.7M by a 2028 exit) and a 20% volume shortfall. Its gates carry numeric thresholds and if-missed actions, and its retail trigger demands a right-sized plan inside the guardrails. Y has one sharper Japan insight: Japan returns more cash than Option A above 25.9% ACoS, so at the pilot's 28% Japan already wins on cash, and Y names Japan as the fallback if the ACoS gate fails. But Y's gates are thinner, with no volume or stall gate, and its retail gate keeps the $10M threshold although its own analysis shows national retail at that point breaks the constraints.

evidence.reasons: Both are numerically accurate on the critical calculations: unit contributions of $10.73 and $4.73/$4.01/$3.05, retail $7.55, Option A cumulative cash of +$2.4M/+$0.4M/−$2.3M at 25/28/32% ACoS, break-even ACoS 28.6% (26.9% with the tariff), Option B peak −$20.8M and 4.5% group margin. Both reject the correlation-based halo, check 4.5 units per door against the awareness bands and the 4.0 delisting bar, exclude the $5.2B figure, and note the two stalled Amazon-first peers. X uses more of the evidence. It gives the CAGR (17.3% vs 5.1%, and 3.5% for the rest of the category), a sell-through-by-halo grid showing the retail gap is structural (halo needed 1.6× to fit the cap, 3.1× to pay back), group-margin headroom, and stall, volume and FX sensitivities. X also makes more speculative moves: a linear extrapolation of the pilot to 333k units, an illustrative 23% growth path to $40M by 2032, and the '1% share' framing. All are flagged and none carries the recommendation. Y makes fewer speculative claims and adds the useful 25.9% Japan indifference point and the '32 units a door' break-even, but it has one unsupported assertion ('fees and product cost are fixed by contract') and does not compute growth as a CAGR.

revision.reasons: The key expects the CEO's hypothesis to be kept with conditions. X handles it most explicitly. It breaks the hypothesis into seven testable conditions, keeps the 2027 Amazon launch, marks 2030 payback 'at risk' with an ACoS gate, and rejects the specific 2029 retail trigger (>$10M, >15% awareness) on the evidence: the 10–20% band sells 3.5 units per door, below the 4.0 bar, and national retail in 2029 cuts group margin to 6.0%. It replaces that trigger with >20% awareness, Amazon ≥$20M and a plan that fits the guardrails, and it re-phases the ambition. Y also keeps the Amazon launch behind an ACoS gate, raises the awareness trigger to 20% and shows national retail in 2029 leaves the US $11.9M short. But it treats the hypothesis less systematically, keeps the $10M sales threshold unchanged, and leaves the retail step as 'needs its own case' rather than a revised condition.

overall.reasons: Both documents are strong and reach the same defensible conclusion with correct core numbers. Y is more concise, and its Japan indifference point (25.9% ACoS) and Japan-as-fallback are useful framing. X would serve the board better: it gives five concrete decisions to approve, a sized cash envelope ($4M), gates with thresholds and if-missed actions, a quantified stall and exit case, an explicit choice between re-phasing the ambition and relaxing the guardrails, and a structural demonstration that no plausible sell-through or halo rescues retail-led. Its extra extrapolations are flagged as illustrative and do not drive the recommendation.
